lesson.title: Beyond Two Choices: Multiple Alleles and Blood Type
lesson.summary: Some genes have more than two alleles circulating in a population, and the human ABO blood type gene, with three alleles combining both dominance and codominance, is the classic example.
lesson.body:
Every cross covered so far has involved a gene with just two possible alleles, one dominant and one recessive. Any single individual only ever carries two alleles for a given gene, one on each chromosome copy, but that does not mean only two versions of that gene exist anywhere in the population. Many genes have three, four, or more different allele versions in circulation, and the ABO blood type gene in humans is the standard teaching example.

The ABO gene has three common alleles: I-A, I-B, and i. The dominance relationships among them combine two ideas from earlier chapters. I-A and I-B are each dominant over i. But I-A and I-B are codominant with each other, exactly like the roan cattle alleles, so a person carrying one of each expresses both. Working through every combination gives six possible genotypes producing four possible phenotypes: I-A I-A or I-A i both give blood type A, I-B I-B or I-B i both give blood type B, I-A I-B gives blood type AB, and only ii gives blood type O.

A worked cross shows how surprising the outcomes can be. Take a parent with blood type A whose genotype is I-A i, and a parent with blood type B whose genotype is I-B i. The type A parent produces I-A and i gametes in equal proportion, and the type B parent produces I-B and i gametes in equal proportion. Combining them gives offspring in four equally likely classes: one quarter I-A I-B, blood type AB, one quarter I-A i, blood type A, one quarter I-B i, blood type B, and one quarter ii, blood type O. A mother with type A blood and a father with type B blood can therefore have children with any of all four possible blood types, which is not something a simple two allele model would predict.

It helps to keep the two ideas separate. Multiple alleles describes how many different versions of a gene exist across a population. Dominance and codominance describe how any two of those alleles behave when they happen to be paired together inside one individual. The ABO gene is memorable precisely because it shows both phenomena working together in a single, medically important system.
